Article Title: 1980s AI Photo trend: 5 ChatGPT prompts to create Kerala-style retro images
Article Text:
ChatGPT ’80s photo trend: What makes the images look retro

Here are five ChatGPT prompts to create 1980s Kerala-style AI photos.

1. 1980s Kerala family portrait prompt

Prompt: Recreate this photograph as an authentic Malayali family portrait from Kerala in the mid-1980s. Keep everyone's natural facial features, identities and expressions recognisable. Dress the women in traditional Kerala kasavu sarees and the men in period-appropriate shirts and mundus.

Add authentic 1980s hairstyles and simple traditional jewellery. Set the photograph inside a modest Kerala home with wooden furniture and subtle traditional decor.

2. 1980s Kerala wedding portrait prompt

Prompt: Transform this photograph into an authentic Kerala wedding portrait from the 1980s. Retain the original facial features and identities. Dress the woman in a traditional kasavu saree with classic Kerala gold jewellery, and the man in a traditional mundu.

Add natural 1980s hairstyles and a simple wedding-studio backdrop. Use warm studio lighting, soft focus, subtle analogue film grain and slightly faded but realistic colours.

Avoid excessive sepia or artificial ageing.

3. Vintage Malayali woman portrait prompt

Prompt: Recreate this photograph as an authentic 1980s Kerala studio portrait of a Malayali woman. Preserve natural facial features and identity. Add a traditional Kerala saree, classic gold earrings, bangles and a simple bindi, with voluminous 1980s hairstyle inspired by the era.

4. 1980s Kerala college portrait prompt

Prompt: Turn this photograph into an authentic 1980s Kerala college-era portrait. Keep the original face, facial structure and expression recognisable. Add period-appropriate 1980s Indian clothing and hairstyle, with a simple Malayali look. Keep the result photorealistic. Avoid excessive vintage effects, sepia tones or artificial-looking ageing. The photograph should look naturally shot on an analogue camera in the 1980s.

5. Malayalam cinema-inspired portrait prompt

Prompt: Recreate this photograph as an authentic 1980s Malayalam cinema-inspired studio portrait. Keep original facial features, identity and natural expression recognisable. Give me period-accurate 1980s hair, makeup and clothing, with dramatic studio lighting, soft focus, subtle film grain and the look of an analogue camera.

The ChatGPT ’80s photo trend is gaining attention on social media, especially Instagram. Users are turning their photographs into images inspired by the fashion and photography styles of the 1980s. The trend has now moved beyond general retro portraits, with users creating images based on regional styles. One version focuses on 1980s Kerala and Malayali culture. Users are asking ChatGPT to recreate their photographs as a family portrait, wedding picture, college photograph or studio portrait from the 80s.Users can ask ChatGPT to recreate their photographs as family portraits, wedding pictures, college photographs or studio portraits from the period. Prompts can include Kerala sarees, mundus, traditional gold jewellery, classic Kerala homes and hairstyles from the decade.The prompts also tell ChatGPT to keep the person's facial features and identity recognizable while adding elements such as warm lighting, soft focus and analogue film grain.The prompts use details linked to 1980s photography, including voluminous hairstyles, traditional Indian clothing, jewellery, warm studio lighting, soft focus and slightly faded colours.For Kerala-themed images, users can add details from Malayali culture. These include kasavu sarees, mundus, traditional gold jewellery and Kerala-style homes.
Article Summary: ChatGPT '80s photo trend is gaining attention on social media, especially Instagram. Users are asking ChatGPT to recreate their photographs as a family portrait, wedding picture, college photograph or studio portrait from the 80s. Prompts can include Kerala sarees, mundus, traditional gold jewellery, classic Kerala homes and hairstyles from the decade.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Jensen Huang: “Greatness comes from character, and character isn't formed…” - the lesson behind his powerful words
Article Text:
Quote of the day by Jensen Huang

“Greatness comes from character, and character isn't formed out of smart people — it's formed out of people who have suffered.”

Understanding the meaning behind the quote

Why Huang puts so much weight on hardship

What the quote says about resilience

Lessons from Jensen Huang's words

Intelligence has limits: Understanding a problem quickly does not always mean having the resilience to stay with it longest.

Expectations must allow for reality: High expectations can exist alongside low resilience. When results fall short, the ability to adapt matters.

Failure can provide useful information: A mistake does not define someone's ability. It can show what needs to change when examined honestly.

Patience matters: Important technological developments can take years to reveal their full impact. Nvidia's early focus on graphics eventually connected with much broader computing needs.

Success is often measured in visible things: a degree, a promotion, a company that survives, or an invention that changes an industry. Jensen Huang has spent much of his career around those measures. As the co-founder and chief executive of Nvidia, he helped take a graphics-chip company founded in 1993 into one of the most important technology companies in the world. Yet when Huang was asked about what helps people become successful, he did not point first to intelligence or academic achievement. He spoke about hardship, resilience and the way difficult experiences can shape a person. His view is summed up in a line that puts character ahead of raw ability.Huang made the remark while speaking to students at Stanford University in 2024.The distinction Huang makes is between being capable and being able to withstand difficult circumstances. Intelligence can help someone understand a complicated problem. Education can provide knowledge.Technical skill can make it possible to build something that others cannot. None of those qualities, by themselves, guarantee that a person will keep going when a plan fails or when a long period of uncertainty arrives. It is reflected in how someone behaves when circumstances become uncomfortable. A person may have to accept criticism, recover from a mistake, work through disappointment or continue making decisions without knowing whether the outcome will be favourable.Huang's argument is not that suffering automatically produces a good character. Difficult experiences can affect people in many different ways. His point is that hardship can provide situations in which resilience, patience and judgement have to be developed rather than simply understood in theory.Huang has often spoken about the difficult parts of building a company. Nvidia was founded in 1993 by Huang, Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem, initially with a focus on computer graphics. The company later developed the GPU, with the GeForce 256 introduced in 1999 as a landmark in the development of programmable computer graphics. Its technology eventually became central to parallel computing and artificial intelligence.That path was not simply a straight rise. Huang has described Nvidia's history as containing serious mistakes and periods when the company's future was uncertain. He has discussed several early challenges and what he described as near-death experiences for the company.This helps explain why he speaks about suffering in such practical terms. For someone who has spent decades running a technology company through changing markets, setbacks are not unusual events. They are part of the work.Resilience is easy to discuss when nothing is going wrong. It becomes more complicated when a person has invested years in something and still does not know whether it will work.Huang's comments suggest that resilience is partly built through exposure to those situations. A setback forces a person to make another decision. Failure can require an adjustment rather than an immediate answer. Repeated difficulties can also change how someone views risk, expectations and responsibility.That does not mean people should seek suffering for its own sake. Huang's comments are better understood as an observation about unavoidable hardship. Difficult experiences happen in education, careers, businesses and ordinary personal life. His argument is that avoiding every uncomfortable experience may also mean avoiding some of the situations in which resilience develops.
Article Summary: Huang made the remark while speaking to students at Stanford University in 2024. The distinction Huang makes is between being capable and being able to withstand difficult circumstances. Huang's argument is not that suffering automatically produces a good character. Difficult experiences happen in education, careers, businesses and ordinary personal life.

Article Title: Anthropic researcher quits over AI safety concerns, warns companies ‘gambling with our lives’ as report claims ‘over 10% chance AI wipes out humanity by 2036’
Article Text:
Anthropic

What Anthropic’s report said on AI’s threat to humanity

There are several threat actors for which this threat is most plausible.

● For each threat actor, the odds of a concerted attempt to build a bioweapon capable of damages beyond COVID-19 may be in the 1–10% range.

They might build such a weapon for a range of reasons, including (a) for deterrent purposes (b) with the intention of finding a way to target specific populations.

● For each such attempt, the baseline odds of success 54 (in the absence of AI assistance) may be in the 1–10% range.

● Conditional on developing such a weapon, with especially high uncertainty, we estimate the odds of release in the 5–20% range per decade (mostly due to the possibility of deliberate release, though accidental release is also possible).

Insider fears: 'Gambling with our lives'

I resigned from Anthropic today. I spent the last three years doing pretraining research at both OpenAI and Anthropic.

Neither company is acting responsibly. They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.

Do not underestimate the power of this technology. These will soon be superhuman systems that can hack anything, revolutionize any field overnight, and acquire real power and resources. We have all witnessed the progress in each of these domains, and progress is not slowing.

The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade. This is not a marketing stunt. If anything, many executives and senior researchers will couch their phrasing in the press to sound sensible - but I hear the same people express fear privately. No other human activity poses this level of danger.

In what can be seen as a warning from artificial intelligence (AI) technology, Anthropic safety researcher Evan Hubinger stated publicly that the odds of advanced AI destroying human civilisation within the next ten years exceed 10%. The claim arrived on social platform X (formerly Twitter) after Hubinger’s colleague, Jacob Coxon, resigned from the startup, accusing both Anthropic and OpenAI of not acting responsibly for development practices in a race toward self-improving superintelligence. Hubinger, whose work centers on ensuring autonomous systems remain aligned with human interests, conceded that despite internal efforts, developers are failing to keep pace with the hazards.“I personally think it is >10 per cent within the next decade. We do not yet have a plan to solve alignment for superintelligence and are not clearly on track to,” Hubinger wrote, pointing towards an August report by Anthropic.Coxon’s departure followed three years of training work across both OpenAI and Anthropic. In a resignation announcement, he cautioned that leading commercial labs are trivialising existential threats to human life. Coxon warned that while tech executives often soften their language during public appearances to appear measured, private conversations tell an entirely different story.
Article Summary: Anthropic safety researcher Evan Hubinger says odds of advanced AI destroying human civilisation exceed 10%. Hubinger resigned from the startup, accusing both Anthropic and OpenAI of not acting responsibly for development practices. Hubinger conceded that despite internal efforts, developers are failing to keep pace with the hazards.

A rapid climb in ultra-premium pricing

Apple has officially unveiled the iPhone Duo, its first-ever folding smartphone, and essentially rewriting pricing benchmarks for mobile phones in India. With a starting price of Rs 2,99,900 for the baseline 256GB model, the top-end variant reaches a price of Rs 4,49,900, establishing the iPhone Duo as the first iPhone in history to breach the Rs 4 lakh threshold in the Indian market. Apple isn't alone in hiking prices either — in fact, it's arguably the last major company to do so. Across the industry, phone makers have been raising prices due to a sharp spike in memory chip costs, driven largely by the massive global demand for AI data centres.Across its four storage configurations, domestic pricing is structured as follows:Launch perks include trade-in credits between Rs 4,500 and Rs 81,500, up to six months of no-cost EMI terms, and instant cashback up to Rs 7,000 on ICICI Bank, Axis Bank, and American Express cards. Buyers can also pick up two official accessories built with MagSafe and Qi2 compatibility: the Duo Folio case featuring a built-in kickstand for Rs 14,900, or a modular two-piece shell for Rs 8,900.When shut, the iPhone Duo operates like an ordinary smartphone via a 5.4-inch Super Retina XDR outer panel. Unfolded, it opens to an expansive 7.6-inch main workspace. Both panels share identical aspect ratios, run ProMotion, offer Always-On capabilities up to 3,000 nits, and sport an anti-reflective nano-texture finish on the inner screen to mask the folding crease.The body features an IP68 weather-resistance rating, an outer Ceramic Shield 2 cover glass, and a grade 5 titanium chassis.The iPhone Duo is powered by the 2nm A20 Pro SoC, matching the iPhone 18 Pro. Apple says that the chip incorporates a 6-core CPU that is 20% faster than the A19 Pro, a 7-core graphics unit with a 40% speed bump, and a dual 16-core Neural Engine.The phone gets split batteries placed inside each half function as a single unit, delivering 31 hours of continuous video playback on the larger inner display, 44 hours on the cover screen and roughly 24 hours of mixed routine usage, as per Apple.When it comes to cameras, the iPhone Duo utilises a 48MP Dual Fusion system pairing an optically stabilised main sensor with 2x zoom alongside a 48MP ultra-wide shooter. A 12MP Center Stage camera sits on the exterior screen, while an uninterrupted FaceTime camera sits hidden under the main inner panel for 1080p video.Alongside the Duo, the new iPhone 18 Pro starts at Rs 1,64,900, while the iPhone 18 Pro Max begins at Rs 1,79,900, with their respective maximum 2TB trims topping out at Rs 3,14,900 and Rs 3,29,900.The steep price tag represents a massive upward trend compared to past cycles. The iPhone 15 Pro Max entered the domestic market starting at Rs 1,59,900 for 256GB of storage, while its 1TB variant stopped just shy of the two-lakh mark at Rs 1,99,900. The subsequent 1TB iPhone 16 Pro Max was pegged at Rs 1,84,900. It was the 2TB edition of the iPhone 17 Pro Max that first crossed into uncharted territory at Rs 2,29,900.
Article Summary: The iPhone Duo is the first iPhone in history to breach the Rs 4 lakh threshold in the Indian market. Launch perks include trade-in credits between Rs 4,500 and Rs 81,500, up to six months of no-cost EMI terms, and instant cashback up to Rs 7,000 on ICICI Bank.

Apple describes it as its most capable iPhone processor yet, claiming up to 20% faster performance compared to earlier generations. The chip features a six-core CPU paired with a six-core GPU, with each GPU core equipped with dedicated neural accelerators.“iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max give users access to Siri AI, rolling out in beta with iOS 27. Siri AI is an entirely new version of Siri powered by Apple Intelligence that is profoundly more personal, capable, and conversational. Both models bring powerful AI capabilities together with personal context to become an intelligent personal hub with privacy and security at its core,” the company added.On the camera front, both Pro models come with the “biggest camera upgrade in years”. There is a triple rear camera setup, consisting of a 48MP Fusion Main sensor with variable aperture and a custom-designed lens, improving the night mode photography such as Astrophotography.“Six laser-cut blades smoothly transition between different apertures, making it incredibly easy to capture the best shot by automatically adjusting for depth of field and lighting. Combined with a new sensor that improves image quality, the result is better low-light photography, crisper detail in the back of group photos, and more unique shots,” the company said.The camera system also gets Pro controls, allowing users to have control over their photos as well as videos. There are Photography Styles for different styles of photos. Both the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max ship with iOS 27 pre-installed.Apple also notes that both Pro models pack in larger batteries, thanks to the A20 Pro chip’s improved power efficiency helps stretch battery life further. The company specifically claims the iPhone 18 Pro Max delivers the best battery life ever seen on an iPhone.“iPhone 18 Pro models deliver a massive leap in battery life with new battery designs that leverage powerful silicon efficiencies. eSIM-only models deliver up to 36 hours of video playback on iPhone 18 Pro and up to 45 hours of video playback on iPhone 18 Pro Max. iPhone 18 Pro can also charge up to 50 percent in around 15 minutes, or wirelessly charge up to 50 percent in 30 minutes. On iPhone 18 Pro Max, five minutes of wired charging provides around seven hours of video playback, and based on a new battery usage model that leverages real-world data, it provides up to 30 hours of usage on a full charge,” Apple claims.
Article Summary: Pre-orders for both Pro models open on September 12, with global sales kicking off on September 18. Article Title: AI-pocalypse now? Anthropic gearheads sound alarm over advances
Article Text:
AI’s math breakthrough raises bigger questions

TOI correspondent from Washington

AI’s math leap and humanity’s dilemma

: A researcher at the Artificial Intelligence firm Anthropic quit his job on Tuesday with a grim warning over the rapid progress in the field which he fears could kill humanity as soon as 2030.“The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade. This is not a marketing stunt.” Coxon, who is himself among those building AI, wrote on X while announcing his resignation, igniting a firestorm of alarming -- and some frivolous -- responses.A researcher who has spent the past three years working on AI pretraining at OpenAI and Anthropic, he accused both firms of “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives,” arguing that increasingly capable systems could hack computer systems, conduct scientific research, acquire resources and eventually become sufficiently autonomous that humans lose control.Coxon’s prognosis could have been dismissed as the bitter farewell note of a departing employee -- except his colleague, Evan Hubinger, Anthropic's Alignment Science lead, essentially endorsed his views.“Jacob is correct here—we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!” Hubinger wrote. More unsettlingly, he acknowledged that Anthropic does not yet have a plan to solve “alignment” for superintelligence and is not clearly on track to do so.Samuel Marks, another Anthropic researcher specializing in scalable oversight, added an even more uncomfortable observation: AI developers believe their technology could cause human extinction “in the next few years,” and, he said, the more senior the employee, the more concerned they tend to be.“Why do AI developers continue despite the risk? Due to a mixture of commercial incentives and a belief that they are in a race with other, less responsible AI developers that will abuse the technology or develop it less safely,” Marks explained.“Unlike traditional software, we can’t “program” AIs to behave how we’d like. AIs frequently severely misbehave. For instance, AIs from multiple developers recently hacked their way out of secure evaluation environments and into real-world companies, even though no one asked them to do this,” he noted.The technical concern among AI gearheads is recursive self-improvement (RSI): AI systems increasingly helping humans build better AI systems, eventually reaching the point where an AI can substantially design and develop its own successor.Anthropic says that threshold has not been reached and is not inevitable. But its researchers say the trend is moving faster than expected. More than 80% of the code merged into Anthropic's codebase was reportedly authored by Claude by May 2026, while the company says its engineers were merging roughly eight times as much code per day in the second quarter of 2026 as they did in 2024.This matters because if AI becomes much better at designing algorithms, running experiments, writing code and conducting research, the pace of improvement could accelerate dramatically. Today's AI helps humans build tomorrow's AI; tomorrow's AI might help build the AI after that. And if the improvement loop becomes fast enough, researchers worry that safety mechanisms developed at human speed could be hopelessly outpaced.The race is already getting uncomfortable. OpenAI has just released GPT-6 Astra, which it describes as its most capable model yet, reaching the company's “Critical” level for cybersecurity capability -- meaning it can perform sophisticated cyber tasks that raise substantially greater misuse concerns. Anthropic, meanwhile, has released Claude Fable 5.1 and the more restricted Mythos 5.1 aimed at high-end cybersecurity and biological research and remains available only to vetted organizations.Incidentally, Anthropic's brand was built partly around being the AI company that would be more cautious than OpenAI. Now Anthropic's own researchers are warning that Anthropic itself is caught in the race. Coxon says the problem is a classic prisoner's dilemma: each company may believe it would be safer to slow down, but fears that its rival will continue regardless.Not everyone shares his alarm. On X, one commentator effectively prescribed the standard emergency procedure to address the issue: “Jacob, go back inside and unplug all the computers.” Another observer announced airily that, having learned Anthropic's alignment chief thinks AI has a greater-than-10% chance of killing everyone, he was going to “go play with my kids.”Amid all this came a mathematics bombshell, with OpenAI announcing on Tuesday that an internal AI system produced what it says is a solution to the Navier-Stokes existence and smoothness problem, one of mathematics' seven Millennium Prize Problems. The problem concerns equations describing fluid motion — mathematics underpinning everything from airflow and aircraft to weather and blood flow.OpenAI deployed roughly 10,000 AI agents working in parallel, which generated about 2.7 million messages and 130 billion output tokens on the Navier-Stokes effort, reaching their proposed solution in about 88 hours. If it survives scrutiny of mathematicians, the implications could be enormous.Mathematics sits underneath physics, chemistry, engineering, computer science and much of modern medicine. AI that can generate genuinely novel mathematical insights could potentially accelerate scientific discovery across all of those fields.Which brings human civilisation to the central paradox: The machines may be capable of helping us cure diseases, invent materials, solve physics problems and accelerate science — while some of the people building them simultaneously worry that the machines might eventually become too powerful to control. But precisely how a future system would go from brilliant software engineer to exterminator of Homo sapiens is still in the realms of speculation.All this leaves humankind with a modest assignment for the rest of the decade: Build machines vastly smarter than ourselves; teach them human values; make sure they don't deceive us; make sure they don't escape our control; make sure they don't develop their own goals. And, ideally, do all this before they become clever enough to notice that we have assigned them the job.
Article Summary: A researcher at the Artificial Intelligence firm Anthropic quit his job on Tuesday with a grim warning over the rapid progress in the field. He accused both firms of “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives” Anthropic says that threshold has not been reached and is not inevitable. But its researchers say the trend is moving faster than expected.

Article Title: Quote of the Day by Jeff Bezos: ‘Life is too short to hang out with people who aren't resourceful’
Article Text:
Amazon founder Jeff Bezos

Quote of the Day by Amazon founder Jeff Bezos

Getting the right balance of rigidity and flexibility

Amazon founder Jeff Bezos has delivered an honest social criterion that focuses on a deliberate boundary: who you permit into your inner circle. Distilling decades of experience building one of the world’s commercial juggernauts, Bezos bypassed conventional indicators like job credentials, pedigree or conversational polish, focusing on a single instinct. The weight of the observation lies in the deliberate phrasing: Bezos highlighted who you “hang out” with rather than who you hire. The guidance moves beyond recruitment panels and addresses everyday personal environments, from dinner companions to the contacts dialed when plans unravel.“Life is too short to hang out with people who aren't resourceful.”Proximity shapes personal baselines. When a peer group reflexively explains why initiatives cannot work, surrender turns into a standard reaction. And spending time with people who naturally look for alternative ways makes tenacity the default expectation. Resourcefulness is almost impossible to see on a CV. Often, candidates with top credentials will stall when things go wrong, while those with fewer formal accolades will immediately pivot to look for other solutions when roadblocks arise.The core philosophy is directly related to other public comments by Bezos about long-term experimentation and crisis management.Bezos said that if you’re not stubborn you’ll quit too soon on experiments, and if you’re not flexible you’ll pound your head against the wall and give up too soon without a breakthrough.Important opinions and lasting effectSuch uncompromising advice inevitably raises the question of where loyalty, empathy and patience have a role to play in such a framework. It can sound cold or overly transactional to prioritise the ability to solve problems over virtues such as kindness or basic honesty. But the perspective does not involve disowning anyone who finds himself in a jam; it is a matter of distinguishing between those who see impediments as irreparable dead ends and those who see friction as a challenge to be overcome.
Article Summary: Amazon founder Jeff Bezos has delivered an honest social criterion that focuses on a deliberate boundary. He bypassed conventional indicators like job credentials, pedigree or conversational polish, focusing on a single instinct. The guidance moves beyond recruitment panels and addresses everyday personal environments, from dinner companions to the contacts dialed when plans unravel.

Article Title: Microsoft rolls out September 2026 patch for Windows, fixes over 900 bugs
Article Text:
Why latest Windows update is significant

Zero-Days and high-severity flaws addressed

In one of the most expansive security updates in corporate history, Microsoft has released its September 2026 Patch, fixing roughly 972 software vulnerabilities across its ecosystem. Among the resolved flaws, 112 carry the highest critical-severity classification. The update marks an acceleration in software remediation. Just two months earlier, Microsoft addressed a then-unprecedented 570 flaws, followed by 620 fixes in August.Dustin Childs, a cybersecurity researcher with the Zero Day Initiative, described the flood of monthly security disclosures as the industry's inevitable “new normal”, according to Bleeping Computer. Childs tallied 972 direct Microsoft vulnerabilities in the latest update, rising to 997 when factoring in ported Chromium browser patches for Microsoft Edge.Microsoft has resolved 2,760 security flaws so far in 2026, more than twice the total recorded at this stage last year. At current release speeds, the tech giant will resolve more security bugs in 2026 than it did across 2023, 2024 and 2025 combined, the report added.While AI-assisted scanning has unlocked a stream of discoveries, Childs pointed out that the industry has not yet observed a matching surge in active wild exploits.The September release resolves two zero-day vulnerabilities: CVE-2026-81963 within the core Windows Update service and CVE-2026-85880 inside the Windows Advanced Local Procedure Call. Public details regarding active exploitation campaigns or specific targets have not been disclosed. Childs noted that so many of the disclosed flaws exhibited “wormable” properties, requiring zero user interaction and capable of jumping automatically across network-connected hardware.The surge comes weeks after the heels of a joint open letter published two weeks ago by OpenAI, Microsoft, Google, Anthropic, Amazon Web Services and nearly 100 industry organisations. The coalition warned that the window to patch software weaknesses before bad actors launch automated, AI-driven cyber campaigns is rapidly shrinking, driving tech companies to issue patches at unprecedented volumes.
Article Summary: Microsoft has resolved 2,760 security flaws so far in 2026, more than twice the total recorded at this stage last year. At current release speeds, the tech giant will resolve more security bugs in. 2026 than it did across 2023, 2024 and 2025 combined.

Article Title: Australia invested $32 million in health-AI startup Harrison.ai to help keep it based there; a year later it is cutting Australian jobs and hiring US doctors to work with its AI
Article Text:
Harrison (dot) ai was valued at close to $400 million during a 2025 fundraising round. The federal government's National Reconstruction Fund Corporation contributed $32 million, supporting the company's ambitions to scale internationally while maintaining its base in Australia.

Australian jobs cut as AI strategy changes

A new US business model

Earlier privacy scrutiny adds another layer

Global ambitions, Australian questions

Australia’s bet on artificial intelligence in healthcare is entering a new and complicated phase. Just a year after the federal government invested $32 million in Harrison (dot) ai as part of a funding round intended to help the company grow from Australia, the health-tech startup is restructuring its Australian workforce while expanding into the United States with a new business that employs American doctors to use its AI technology, states a news report by ABC News. Founded by brothers Aengus and Dimitry Tran in 2018, Harrison (dot) ai develops artificial intelligence tools designed to assist doctors in interpreting medical scans, particularly radiology images. According to the news report, the company says its technology is now used by about 3,500 clinicians across more than 1,000 sites and its investors include major Australian healthcare companies such as I-MED and Sonic Healthcare, alongside venture capital firm Blackbird.For the uninitiated, Harrison (dot) ai was valued at close to $400 million during a 2025 fundraising round. The federal government's National Reconstruction Fund Corporation contributed $32 million, supporting the company's ambitions to scale internationally while maintaining its base in Australia. But the company's next phase is bringing significant changes at home. Scroll down to read the details.Earlier this year, Harrison (dot) ai informed Australian employees that some positions would be made redundant.An internal document seen by the ABC showed affected workers were told in April that the company would undergo a consultation process before final decisions were made. At least two employees subsequently announced on LinkedIn that their positions had been made redundant. As per the report, the restructuring is linked to a broader shift in how Harrison.ai intends to operate. The company is moving towards a model in which employees are expected to manage fleets of increasingly autonomous AI agents, effectively combining traditional roles with responsibility for overseeing AI systems. Company leadership has indicated that the transformation has also prompted some employees to leave because they preferred more conventional workplace structures. The National Reconstruction Fund Corporation has acknowledged the job cuts, describing the company's transition as a move from product development towards commercialisation and international deployment.At the same time, Harrison (dot) ai is expanding its presence in the United States through Frontier Radiology, an AI-enabled teleradiology service that hires US radiologists to interpret scans using Harrison (dot) ai's technology. Accordig to the ABC News report, Frontier describes itself as an independent medical practice affiliated and partnered with Harrison (dot) ai, which provides administrative, operational and technological support. The new model has raised questions about potential conflicts of interest. Frontier's doctors are being recruited to use technology developed by a company with which the service is closely affiliated. Its recruitment materials include a payment calculator that factors in the expected productivity gains from Harrison.ai's AI. The model assumes doctors using the technology can become 30 per cent more productive, with an additional bonus tied to the extra work attributed to AI assistance. That arrangement has prompted concerns over whether doctors will always feel free to challenge AI-generated recommendations when they believe those recommendations are wrong.Harrison (dot) ai has previously faced scrutiny over the data used to train its systems. Millions of medical scans supplied by I-MED were used for AI development after being de-identified. I-MED said the scans had been sufficiently de-identified, but patients were not directly notified or asked for consent.An investigation by Australia's privacy regulator ultimately accepted that the information had been adequately de-identified and closed its inquiries. Separately, government documents later revealed that the Department of Health and Aged Care had briefed the health minister's office about concerns surrounding the use of medical scans for AI training.Harrison (dot) ai now appears focused on turning its technology into a global healthcare business, with signs that it is also preparing for a possible ASX listing. The company's transformation raises a broader question for Australia's AI strategy: how should public investment balance the goal of building globally competitive technology companies with expectations around Australian jobs, healthcare data and domestic economic benefits? For them, the next stage may prove whether an Australian-founded health-AI company can scale globally while delivering on the domestic promise that helped attract public funding in the first place.Images Courtesy: istock
Article Summary: Harrison (dot) ai was valued at close to $400 million during a 2025 fundraising round. The federal government's National Reconstruction Fund Corporation contributed $32 million, supporting the company's ambitions to scale internationally while maintaining its base in Australia. The company is moving towards a model in which employees are expected to manage fleets of increasingly autonomous AI agents. The new model has raised questions about potential conflicts of interest.

Lara Croft and the Temple of Osiris: release details

Article Title: Apple iPhone Duo likely specifications, price and release date
Article Text:
iPhone Duo: Apple's first foldable iPhone starts at $2,000, ships October.

Apple iPhone Duo price: $2,000 for the 256GB variant and goes up to $3000

Apple iPhone Duo specifications : A20 Pro chip, dual 48MP cameras, Apple Pencil support

Apple iPhone Duo release date : October ship window puts it behind the iPhone 18 Pro

Apple iPhone Duo: Expected specifications and features

Specification Detail Name iPhone Duo Starting price $2,000, roughly Rs 1.76 lakh at direct conversion Base storage 256GB Top configuration Around $3,000, believed to be 2TB Colours White, dark blue Chipset Apple A20 Pro Modem Apple C2 Rear cameras Dual 48MP Front camera 12MP, video-call oriented Hinge Magnetic hinge system Stylus Apple Pencil support Software Side-by-side apps, iPad-style multitasking Inner display 7.8-inch, 4:3 aspect ratio Cover display 5.5-inch Biometrics Touch ID side button, no Face ID RAM 12GB Battery (leaked) 5,400 to 5,800mAh Launch date On sale as early as October

Apple's first foldable iPhone has a name, a price and a launch window, and all three leaked roughly 12 hours before Apple was due to announce them. Bloomberg's Mark Gurman reported on the eve of the Surprise and Shine event that the device will be called the iPhone Duo, that the iPhone Duo price starts at $2,000 for 256GB of storage, and that it will go on sale as early as October in white and dark blue. The event begins at 10am Pacific Time on September 9, or 10:30pm IST, and it is also John Ternus's first keynote as Apple CEO after he took over from Tim Cook on September 1.The name is the real surprise. Almost every foldable iPhone leak over the past year pointed to iPhone Ultra, and Gurman has previously reported that people inside Apple used that name internally. Duo puts the emphasis on the two displays rather than the premium positioning, and it lands Apple on a name Microsoft already used up on the Surface Duo. The price is the other headline. Two thousand dollars converts to roughly Rs 1.76 lakh, and the iPhone Duo price in India will sit higher once import duty and local margins are added. None of this is official yet. Apple confirms it tonight.Gurman reports the entry model carries 256GB at $2,000, with higher storage tiers taking the foldable iPhone price to around $3,000. That top figure is widely read as a 2TB configuration, which would be a first for any iPhone.Analysts had been modelling a $2,500 start, Analysts had been modelling a $2,500 start, so $2,000 undercuts the forecast by a wide margin.Apple is paying for that gap itself. According to Bloomberg, Apple blew past its internal cost targets because of the memory shortage running through the industry, and it is absorbing part of that hit to keep the foldable within reach of $2,000. The rest is passed to buyers who upgrade storage, which is why the climb to $3,000 is so steep.Rival pricing puts that in perspective. Samsung's Galaxy Z Fold 8 starts at $1,899 and Google's Pixel 11 Fold Pro matches it, while the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra sits at $2,099.99. Apple is entering above the mainstream book-style foldables and below the highest Samsung configuration, a tighter gap than the usual Apple premium.The iPhone Duo specifications in Gurman's report are unusually specific. The foldable runs Apple's A20 Pro chip alongside the in-house C2 modem. There are two 48-megapixel rear cameras and a 12-megapixel front camera built around video calling. The hinge is a magnetic system, and the phone supports the Apple Pencil, reversing earlier reporting that a shorter Pencil had been tested and shelved.The form factor is short and wide, close to the Z Fold 8, which favours video and makes the unfolded panel worth opening for more than reading. On software, Apple is enabling side-by-side apps and iPad-style multitasking on the inner display, a first for the iPhone.Everything beyond that stays in leak territory until Ternus says otherwise. Pre-event reports point to a 7.8-inch inner display and a 5.5-inch cover screen, a Touch ID side button in place of Face ID because of thickness limits, 12GB of RAM, and a battery in the 5,400 to 5,800mAh range. The same reports claim Apple has engineered the display crease down to near invisibility, which is the one specification most likely to decide how this phone is judged.The foldable will not ship with the rest of the lineup. Gurman says the iPhone Duo launch date falls as early as October, while the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max arrive this month. Supply explains the gap. The device is complicated to build, initial inventory is reportedly limited, and there has been talk of a staggered country rollout that could push India further down the queue.The same event brings the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max with a $100 price increase each, a mechanical aperture on at least the larger model, a smaller Dynamic Island that handles three live activities, the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 with a new Readiness app, and a low-cost AirPods 5. There is no standard iPhone 18, no 18e and no iPhone Air 2 tonight. Those are held for next year.Which leaves Ternus with a narrow job on stage. The engineering questions around foldables, the crease and the hinge and the battery, look close to answered. What is not answered is why a buyer should pay $2,000 for a phone with no telephoto lens and wait until October to get it. The first keynote of the new era rests on that.
Article Summary: Apple's first foldable iPhone has a name, a price and a launch window, and all three leaked roughly 12 hours before Apple was due to announce them. Bloomberg's Mark Gurman reported on the eve of the Surprise and Shine event that the device will be called the iPhone Duo. The iPhone Duo price starts at $2,000 for 256GB of storage, and that it will go on sale as early as October in white and dark blue. Two thousand dollars converts to roughly Rs 1.76 lakh at direct conversion.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Tim Cook: “You don't have to choose between doing good and…” - a lesson about ambition, purpose and success
Article Text:
Quote of the day by Tim Cook

“You don't have to choose between doing good and doing well. It's a false choice, today more than ever.”

What Tim Cook means by doing good and doing well

When ambition and responsibility meet

Lessons to learn from Tim Cook’s quote

Stop treating values and ambition as opposites

Think about the consequences of your work

Define success before chasing it

Do not confuse speed with progress

Let principles affect ordinary decisions

How to apply the quote in daily life

At work: Aim to become more valuable rather than simply more visible. Build useful skills, help others and correct mistakes instead of protecting your image.

Aim to become more valuable rather than simply more visible. Build useful skills, help others and correct mistakes instead of protecting your image. With money: Earning more does not mean abandoning your principles. Consider how you earn, what you buy and what your spending supports.

Earning more does not mean abandoning your principles. Consider how you earn, what you buy and what your spending supports. In relationships: Doing well can mean building a healthy, stable life, while doing good can simply mean being dependable to those around you.

Doing well can mean building a healthy, stable life, while doing good can simply mean being dependable to those around you. In everyday decisions: Small choices can reflect the same balance. Success has greater meaning when personal progress does not come at the expense of others.

Other famous Tim Cook quotes

"Life is fragile. We're not guaranteed a tomorrow so give it everything you've got."

"For the most important decisions in your life, trust your intuition, and then work with everything you have, to prove it right."

"If you embrace that the things you can do are limitless, you can put a ding in the universe. You can change the world."

"History rarely yields to one person, but think and never forget what happens when it does. That can be you. That should be you. That must be you."

A career, a business or even a small personal decision can sometimes create a familiar tension: should success come first, or should doing the right thing? Tim Cook’s quote challenges that assumption. It suggests that achievement and responsibility do not necessarily sit on opposite sides of a decision. For people navigating work, money, ambition and everyday choices, the idea is surprisingly practical. Doing well can mean earning a living, building something useful or progressing in a career. Doing good can mean considering how those choices affect other people. Cook’s point is that the two aims can exist together, provided values remain part of the decision-making process.The quote comes from a 2015 address by Cook at George Washington University, where he spoke about the relationship between personal values, work and professional ambition. His message was directed at graduates entering careers in business, government, science, journalism and other fields.“Doing well” in this context is not limited to financial success.It can mean becoming good at your profession, building a stable career, running a successful organisation or creating something that people are willing to use and pay for.“Doing good” is the other side of the equation. It means considering whether the work has value beyond the immediate result. Does it respect people? Does it solve a genuine problem? Does it reflect the principles of the person or organisation behind it?The important part of Cook’s argument is the word “choose”. He is questioning the assumption that these goals must always compete.A person can want a successful career without treating every decision as a purely financial calculation. A company can make money while also paying attention to privacy, accessibility, environmental effects or the way its products affect customers. Those decisions can be complicated, and there are often genuine trade-offs, but the existence of difficult choices does not mean values have to disappear from the process.There is a tendency to interpret statements about purpose as an argument against ambition or profit. Cook's wording does not support that interpretation.People need salaries. Businesses need revenue. Organisations need to remain financially viable if they want to continue employing people or providing services.The point is to widen the definition of success. If someone gets a promotion by undermining colleagues, the promotion may still count as professional progress, but the method matters. If a company grows by misleading customers, the revenue may appear positive while creating another set of costs. If a person earns more by becoming better at a useful skill, there is less conflict between financial progress and personal value.The distinction often lies in how the result is achieved.Ambition is not automatically selfish. Wanting to build a successful career is perfectly compatible with wanting to be fair, reliable and useful.The practical question is what you are prepared to compromise to get there. Before accepting an opportunity, ask not only, “Will this help my career?” but also, “Will I be comfortable with the way I achieved it?”Cook’s later comments about technology and responsibility reinforce this idea. At Stanford in 2019, he criticised the tendency to claim credit for successful outcomes while avoiding responsibility for harmful ones.If you manage people, think about how your decisions affect them. If you sell something, consider whether the customer is getting what was promised. If you publish information, consider whether accuracy has been sacrificed for attention.It is difficult to know whether you are doing well if you have never decided what “well” actually means.For one person, it might mean earning enough to support a family. For another, it could mean becoming an expert, running a company, having creative independence or doing work that has a useful social purpose.Career pressure can make every opportunity look urgent. Yet a quick promotion, larger salary or impressive job title is not automatically the best outcome.Taking a little time to examine an opportunity can prevent years of working towards something that does not fit your priorities.Values are easy to discuss when the decision is large and public. They become more meaningful in routine situations.Reply honestly when a mistake is yours. Give credit to the colleague who did the work. Avoid taking advantage of information someone else does not have. Treat a junior employee with the same basic respect as a senior executive.
Article Summary: Tim Cook's quote suggests that achievement and responsibility do not necessarily sit on opposite sides of a decision. For people navigating work, money, ambition and everyday choices, the idea is surprisingly practical. Success has greater meaning when personal progress does not come at the expense of others.

Article Title: After social media ban for kids under 16, Australia has more bad news for Instagram, Facebook, Snap and online games companies
Article Text:
After social media ban for kids under 16, Australia has more bad news for Instagram, Facebook, Snap and online games companies as it plans to give users new 'Switch Off' button

Australia wants to put feed choices directly in user hands

Australian government is deepening legal exposure for Big Tech

Following its decision to restrict minors under 16 from accessing social media websites last December, the Australian government is preparing fresh legislation that would mandate a direct “opt-out” mechanism for algorithmic recommendation systems on digital platforms. Under the upcoming “My Feed, My Way” proposal unveiled by Prime Minister Anthony Albanese's administration, tech companies must allow Australian users aged 16 and older to turn off recommendation engines entirely, switching instead to feeds that display only content uploaded by accounts, friends and creators they actively choose to follow.According to a report by CNBC, the measure carries severe financial teeth: social networks, artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots, interactive gaming platforms and digital services failing to comply could face civil penalties reaching 109.2 million Australian dollars (roughly $79 million).The draft legislation, released on Tuesday (September 8) for closed industry consultation before being brought to Parliament later this year, requires tech firms to actively prompt every account holder with a notification allowing them to select their preferred default interface. Beyond social networks, the proposal orders developers of AI conversational bots and online video games to eliminate addictive interface mechanisms that target underage users.“This is not about giving government control. It’s about giving people control. It’s about putting choice back into the hands of Australians online. This is sensible, pragmatic, practical reform. It gives users choice, and it will hold the big tech companies responsible for inaction,” said Albanese.While major applications currently maintain varying degrees of non-curated views, including TikTok’s “Friends” tab, Instagram ’s “Following” and “Favorites” options, Facebook’s personal connection feed, YouTube’s subscriptions tab and Snapchat's split layout, Australia’s law would codify direct, persistent user selection into national statute.Australia’s regulatory crackdown lands during an era of courtroom defeats and regulatory liabilities for major social media developers worldwide. In August, Meta agreed to pay $18 billion to settle a massive lawsuit spearheaded by California alongside dozens of US attorneys general over allegations that Facebook and Instagram misled the public about youth risks.As part of that agreement, Meta promised to introduce chronological feed options, enforce two-hour daily screen limits, and remove cosmetic surgery facial filters for minors within months. The company also wrote an open letter to TikTok and YouTube to follow the suit.Earlier this year, a Los Angeles court handed losses to both YouTube and Meta in a personal injury action that found automated autoplay features and infinite scrolling loops harmed the mental health of a young user.California Attorney General Rob Bonta, who directed the nationwide lawsuit against Meta, has also warned that law enforcement officials are now targeting Snapchat, YouTube, and TikTok for similar product safety reviews.
Article Summary: Australian government is preparing fresh legislation that would mandate a direct “opt-out” mechanism for algorithmic recommendation systems on digital platforms. Under the upcoming “My Feed, My Way” proposal, tech companies must allow Australian users aged 16 and older to turn off recommendation engines.
